title: Observations on the Reform of Catholic High School Education https://primematters.com/index.php/perspectives/observations-reform-catholic-high-school-education
author: Matthew C. Briel
summary: Matthew C. Briel offers a critique of the Great Books model within Catholic classical schools and proposes forming the Catholic imagination instead. He credits four decades of classical reform, including the Great Books programs and the trivium and quadrivium schools, for producing well-prepared and faithful graduates. But he argues the standard Great Books approach carries an Enlightenment anthropology that treats students as unfallen, neutral individuals sampling a great conversation, which breeds cynicism. He distinguishes the immediate end of Catholic liberal education, in Newman's sense of seeing the whole of reality, from its ultimate end of salvation, warning against collapsing the school's task into making saints. Drawing on Lewis, Tolkien, Aristotle and Aquinas, he says the imagination presents the good through particulars, so doctrine should be seen incarnated in lives. He concludes that more school time should go to literature and history than to abstract philosophy, preparing the way for God to make saints.

A Catholic school's main task is to form students in a sacramental vision of reality permeated by the Incarnation, not to induct them into a great conversation.
He separates the immediate end of liberal education, knowledge and seeing reality whole, from the ultimate end of salvation, and warns against collapsing a school into a saint-making institution.
Following Lewis, Tolkien, Newman, Aristotle and Aquinas, the imagination reaches the heart through concrete particulars, so literature and history should receive more time than abstract philosophy.
Schools do not inculcate virtue directly but present beautiful lives to imitate, preparing the way for the student to accept or reject the vision.
quotes: At its core, the standard Great Books approach has an Enlightenment anthropology. We expose students to “the great conversation” with all its pitfalls, and leave the student to make what sense he can of it in a community of other readers.

Rather than a Great Books approach, I propose that a Catholic school’s main task is to form students in a vision of reality permeated by the Incarnation. It is a sacramental vision that recognizes that “the world is charged with the grandeur of God
There is a danger in collapsing the Church’s educational apostolate into “making saints.

For Newman, the end of liberal education is seeing the whole of reality. Philosophical knowledge (not the academic discipline of philosophy) is a form of knowledge that synthesizes the views of particular disciplines into a coherent vision of all of reality.

Indeed, I would go so far as to say that most of the time given to traditional philosophy in a Catholic classical school ought to be given to literature and history, and that courses in Catholic doctrine should be less abstract and more literary and historical.

We learn to live a good life by imitation. A central intellectual task for a student to develop in high school is how doctrines, which, again, are true abstractions from scripture, can be seen embodied, incarnated, in particular lives.

It is not that we bring the students into a “great conversation” but rather that we judiciously use “the best that has been thought and said in the world” (including pagan and “heretical” texts but with a preponderance of Catholic texts) to both form and bring students to a Catholic vision of reality.
